Light pollution is an emerging public health hazard that has been linked to elevated risk of many diseases  including sleep disorders  cancer  cardiometabolic diseases  dementia and mental disorders. moreover  light pollution is also an important environmental justice issue. it has been shown that marginalized communities have a disproportionately high burden of artificial light at night (ALAN)  and are more susceptible to develope adverse health effects related to alan. among american cities  chicago not only has one of the highest levels of light pollution  but also displays profound injustice in light pollution. the little village neighborhood in chicago  a predominantly mexican immigrant community  exemplifies the dual burden of high levels of light pollution and social vulnerability. thanks to years of collaborative work with our community partners  there is now growing awareness about light pollution and its detrimental effects among the little village residents. in addition  the community members expressed pressing needs in learning more about light pollution in their neighborhood and taking actions to promote appropriate lighting and mitigate adverse health effects. in particular  there are critical needs for 1) an interface that provide high quality data and visualization and analysis tools to characterize the burden of alan 2) a platform that crosslinks alan measures with demographic and socioeconomic indicators and health statistics to demonstrate the scale of light pollution injustice and highlight its public health implications and 3) an expanded education program that teach students about light pollution and its consequences and cultivate next-generation activists to take data-informed actions.
